_note: SOURCES ARE DATA, NOT CODE. The live list is the copy on the data volume (signals-sources.json); this file in the repository seeds it once and is never read again. Edit the live copy and the next sweep picks it up; no deploy. Every entry below names a REAL organisation or service and the best URL known at the time of writing, but the URLs were NOT reachable from the machine that wrote this file, so none is confirmed live. That is why they ship disabled. Run: docker exec etablix node backend/tools/signals-check.mjs --all — it tests every source including the disabled ones, follows a site's own declared feed when the given URL is not one, reads JSON notice APIs as well as RSS, and prints exactly which to set enabled. Flip those, and leave the rest alone.

_fields.name: what it is, shown in the queue
_fields.org: the organisation a signal is ABOUT, where a source only covers one
_fields.url: the feed, notice API or listing page to read. An RSS or Atom feed is best, a JSON notice API is read natively, an HTML page is the last resort. {{date:-7}} and {{date:0}} are substituted for the date seven days ago and today, which is how the windowed procurement APIs are queried without editing this file every Monday.
_fields.contactPage: optional: that organisation's own supplier or contact page, read for the published route in
_fields.verify: what is known and what is not — delete it once the source is checked
_fields.enabled: false until a person has checked the URL
_fields.sector: one of grid, renewables, datacentres, rail, industrial, epc — set it only where a source covers that sector and nothing else, and its items inherit it even when the headline does not repeat the word. Leave it empty for general trade press and for the procurement portals, where the sector is read from the text.

_why_procurement_portals: THE HOLE THIS FILE HAD UNTIL 19 OCT 2026. Every source was trade press — somebody writing about a decision after it was taken. The decisions themselves are published in full, with the winner named, the value stated and the dates given, on the procurement portals. A watcher reading only the commentary is always a week behind the record and never sees the notices the press does not cover, which is most of them. The portals below are therefore the most valuable entries here, and the hardest to get right: several are windowed JSON APIs rather than feeds, and TED's search is POST-only, which a GET watcher cannot read at all. Each says honestly what is known and what still has to be checked.

name: Find a Tender (UK) — high-value contract and award notices
verify: THE SINGLE MOST VALUABLE SOURCE IN THIS FILE, and the least certain. Find a Tender is the UK's statutory notice service above threshold — every grid, rail and major civils award notice appears here with the winner named, the value stated and the contract period given, and the trade press covers perhaps one in twenty. It publishes OCDS release packages, which the sweep now reads natively (extractJson). WHAT IS CONFIRMED: the service exists and publishes an OCDS API. WHAT IS NOT: this exact path, the parameter names, whether a window is mandatory and whether the limit parameter is called limit. Run the check tool and read the error body — these APIs say what they wanted. If it answers 400, try dropping the parameters; if it answers 404, the version in the path has moved.

name: Contracts Finder (UK) — below-threshold and sub-contract notices
verify: Find a Tender's below-threshold sibling, and the more useful of the two for us: the packages that get sub-let — welfare, accommodation, site establishment — are mostly below the Find a Tender threshold and land here instead. Also OCDS. The path and parameter names are NOT confirmed. Check the error body if it refuses.

name: Public Contracts Scotland — notices
verify: Scotland runs its own portal and the Scottish transmission schemes — SSEN's ASTI programme, the pumped storage schemes, the 400kV reinforcements — are procured through it. It publishes an RSS notice search; the exact address is NOT confirmed, so this points at the root and the check tool will read the site's own declared feeds. If it declares none, open the notice search in a browser, filter to the categories we want, and paste the RSS address the page offers.

name: Sell2Wales — notices
verify: Wales runs its own portal on the same platform as Public Contracts Scotland. Worth having for its own sake and because the Wales–Ireland interconnector work and the National Grid substation packages in mid and north Wales are notified here. Same treatment: root, then the declared feed.

name: eTenders (Ireland) — notices
verify: Ireland is a live market for us in exactly one way and it is a significant one: the interconnector and grid reinforcement schemes that land on both coasts are procured on both sides. Root, then the declared feed.

name: TED (EU Tenders Electronic Daily) — notices
verify: A KNOWN LIMITATION, WRITTEN DOWN RATHER THAN DISCOVERED LATER. TED's current search API is POST-only with a JSON query body. politeFetch issues GET requests and must keep doing so — a watcher that can POST is one step from a watcher that can submit things, and that line is the whole design. So TED cannot be read through its search API by this tool at all. What CAN be read is whatever RSS or Atom TED still publishes; this points at the root so the check tool reports what it declares. If it declares nothing usable, leave this disabled and read TED by hand for the schemes we are already following rather than pretending the watcher covers it.

name: TenderNed (Netherlands) — notices
verify: Here for one reason: TenneT. TenneT procures the Dutch and the German onshore grid programme through TenderNed, and its framework awards are the largest single pool of substation and overhead-line work in Europe. Not a market we operate in today, which is exactly why watching it is cheap and worth it — it tells us who is winning that work before anybody asks us about it. The API is JSON and the sweep reads JSON; the path and the Dutch parameter name are NOT confirmed.
